title: Could You Survive Lost at Sea?
credits: Images: US Coast Guard, US Navy / National Museum of the U.S. Navy, NASA (Goddard, JPL), US Air Force (public domain). Steven Callahan photos by North Yarmouth Academy (CC BY 2.0). Life raft photos: NPL FP2011 (CC BY-SA 3.0), Sillerkiil (CC BY-SA 4.0). Hydration colour chart: Petar Milosevic (CC BY-SA 4.0). Globe texture: NASA Earth Observatory Blue Marble. Video: Pixabay (Pixabay Content License). Facts: Callahan, Adrift (1986); Poon Lim records (US Navy; Imperial War Museums); Alvarenga reports (2014); osmosis and dehydration physiology.

scenes.text: You are floating in a rubber raft in the middle of the ocean. No land, no radio, no one looking. Experts would give you days. Yet three men lasted months. Stay to the end to learn the one thing you must never drink.

scenes.code:
title=Text("THE RULE OF THREES",font_size=46,color=ORANGE).to_edge(UP)
items=[("3 MINUTES","without air"),("3 HOURS","in harsh weather"),("3 DAYS","without water"),("3 WEEKS","without food")]
rows=VGroup()
for i,(a,b) in enumerate(items):
    big=Text(a,font_size=54,color=RED if i==2 else YELLOW)
    sm=Text(b,font_size=34,color=WHITE)
    rows.add(VGroup(big,sm).arrange(RIGHT,buff=0.5,aligned_edge=DOWN))
rows.arrange(DOWN,buff=0.6,aligned_edge=LEFT).move_to(DOWN*0.3)

scenes.text: Survivors use the rule of threes: roughly three minutes without air, three hours in harsh weather, three days without water, three weeks without food.

label: ADRIFT
Day one
scenes.fact: A common rule of thumb: roughly three days\Nwithout water, and less in the heat.
scenes.text: Your raft has already solved the first number, because you are breathing. The clock that matters now is the water clock. And it is ticking.
The first rule on a raft is to stop and think. Ration what you have, stay in the shade, and move as little as you can, because sweat is water.

scenes.text: Your body is more than half water. Lose just two percent and thirst clouds your thinking. Lose ten percent and your organs begin to struggle.

label: DEHYDRATION
The colour gauge
scenes.fact: Dark urine is an early sign of dehydration.
scenes.text: Your first warning is colour. The darker your urine, the more dehydrated you are.

chapter: WHY YOU CAN'T DRINK THE SEA
scenes.text: Thirst makes one idea tempting. You are surrounded by water. So why not just drink it?

scenes.code:
np.random.seed(4)
title=Text("SEAWATER: ABOUT 3.5% SALT",font_size=38,color=YELLOW).to_edge(UP,buff=0.4)
cell=Circle(radius=1.8,color=GREEN,fill_color=GREEN,fill_opacity=0.25,stroke_width=6)
salts=VGroup()
while len(salts)<46:
    p=np.array([np.random.uniform(-6,6),np.random.uniform(-2.3,2.3),0])
    if np.linalg.norm(p)>2.6: salts.add(Dot(p,radius=0.09,color=YELLOW))
water=VGroup()
for k in range(14):
    a=np.random.uniform(0,TAU); r=np.random.uniform(0.2,1.4)
    water.add(Dot(np.array([r*np.cos(a),r*np.sin(a),0]),radius=0.1,color=BLUE))
cl=Text("CELL",font_size=30,color=WHITE).move_to(cell.get_center()+DOWN*0.05)
self.play(Write(title),FadeIn(cell),FadeIn(salts),FadeIn(water),run_time=1.5)
moves=[]
for d in water:
    v=d.get_center(); v=v/ (np.linalg.norm(v)+1e-6)
    moves.append(d.animate.move_to(v*np.random.uniform(2.9,3.6)))
self.play(AnimationGroup(*moves,lag_ratio=0.08),cell.animate.scale(0.55),run_time=3.5)
res=Text("WATER LEAVES THE CELL. IT SHRINKS.",font_size=34,color=RED).to_edge(DOWN,buff=0.4)
self.play(Write(res),run_time=1.2)
self.wait(1.0)
scenes.text: Seawater is about three and a half percent salt. By osmosis, that salt pulls water out of your cells, and they shrink.

scenes.caption: OF SALT IN EVERY LITRE OF SEAWATER
scenes.fact: Human blood is roughly 0.9 percent salt,\Nseawater is nearly four times that.
scenes.text: Your kidneys can only make urine less salty than the sea. To flush the salt from one litre, you need more than a litre of water. Every sip leaves you thirstier.

label: THE SUN
Hits you twice
scenes.text: The sun burns you twice, from above and from the light bouncing off the water.
At night the danger flips. Water pulls heat from your body far faster than air does, so soaked and still in the wind, you slowly chill, even in a tropical sea.

label: STEVEN CALLAHAN
Atlantic, 1982
scenes.text: In 1982, sailor Steven Callahan's small sloop sank in the Atlantic, far from land. He escaped into a tiny inflatable raft.
Something hit his boat in the night, he believed a whale. Water poured in, and he had minutes to grab flares, a spear gun and his solar stills.

scenes.fact: Callahan drifted nearly 3,000 km before\Nfishermen found him near Guadeloupe.
scenes.text: For seventy-six days he drifted. He made solar stills, speared fish that gathered under the raft, and drank rain whenever it fell.
Then his raft began to leak. He spent hours every day pumping and patching it.
He later wrote a bestselling book, Adrift, about those seventy-six days.

label: POON LIM
Atlantic, 1942 to 1943
scenes.fact: Poon Lim: 133 days alone, the longest\Nrecorded solo raft survival.
scenes.text: Poon Lim's ship was torpedoed in 1942. He then spent 133 days alone on a raft.
He fished, caught rain, and Brazilian fishermen found him. The US Navy wanted his secrets.

label: JOSE SALVADOR ALVARENGA
Pacific, 2012 to 2014
scenes.text: Then comes Alvarenga, a Mexican fisherman. In December 2012 a storm killed his engine and radio.

scenes.title: ALVARENGA'S DRIFT
scenes.text: He drifted west for about four hundred and thirty-eight days. His young companion did not survive. At last, in January 2014, the boat reached Ebon Atoll in the Marshall Islands, roughly ten thousand kilometres from where it began.

title=Text("DAYS ADRIFT",font_size=44,color=ORANGE).to_edge(UP,buff=0.4)
data=[("Callahan",76,YELLOW),("Poon Lim",133,ORANGE),("Alvarenga",438,RED)]

    rows.add(lab); bars.add(VGroup(b,v))

self.play(Write(title),FadeIn(rows),run_time=1.0)

scenes.text: Put them side by side: seventy-six days, one hundred and thirty-three days, and four hundred and thirty-eight. All three smashed the three-day rule.
Why so far? Steady trade winds and ocean currents push anything floating in the tropics west, no engine required.

scenes.yt_chapter: How to make fresh water at sea
scenes.text: Option one is rain. Spread any sheet or canopy, and funnel every drop into a container.

scenes.code:
title=Text("SOLAR STILL",font_size=44,color=ORANGE).to_edge(UP,buff=0.4)
pool=Rectangle(width=6.6,height=1.0,fill_color=BLUE,fill_opacity=0.8,stroke_width=0).move_to(DOWN*1.1)
sheet=Polygon(LEFT*3.3+DOWN*0.6,UP*0.7,RIGHT*3.3+DOWN*0.6,color=WHITE,stroke_width=4)
cup=Rectangle(width=0.9,height=0.45,color=GREEN,stroke_width=5).move_to(DOWN*0.3)
sun=Circle(radius=0.5,color=YELLOW,fill_color=YELLOW,fill_opacity=1).move_to(LEFT*5+UP*2)
rays=VGroup(*[Arrow(sun.get_center()+RIGHT*0.6+DOWN*0.3*k,LEFT*2.5+UP*(0.9-0.5*k),color=YELLOW,buff=0.1,stroke_width=4) for k in range(3)])
l1=Text("SEAWATER",font_size=30,color=BLUE).move_to(DOWN*2.4)
self.play(Write(title),FadeIn(pool),Create(sheet),FadeIn(cup),FadeIn(sun),run_time=1.5)
self.play(Create(rays),FadeIn(l1),run_time=1.0)
vap=VGroup(*[Arrow(RIGHT*x+DOWN*0.55,RIGHT*x+UP*0.0,color=RED,buff=0,stroke_width=4) for x in (-2.4,-1.4,1.4,2.4)])
l2=Text("VAPOUR RISES, SALT STAYS",font_size=28,color=RED).move_to(RIGHT*3.5+UP*1.5)
self.play(Create(vap),FadeIn(l2),run_time=1.5)
d=Dot(LEFT*1.6+UP*0.05,color=BLUE,radius=0.09)
self.add(d)
self.play(d.animate.move_to(UP*0.7),run_time=1.0)
self.play(d.animate.move_to(DOWN*0.2),run_time=0.6)
l3=Text("FRESH WATER",font_size=30,color=GREEN).move_to(RIGHT*3.6+DOWN*0.4)
self.play(FadeIn(l3),run_time=0.6)
self.wait(1.0)
scenes.text: Option two: a solar still. Sun evaporates seawater, salt stays behind, and fresh drops collect in a cup. The yield is small.

scenes.code:
title=Text("THE WATER MATH (ILLUSTRATIVE)",font_size=38,color=ORANGE).to_edge(UP,buff=0.4)
data=[("NEED: ~2 L / DAY",4.4,YELLOW),("SOLAR STILL",0.8,BLUE),("ONE HEAVY SQUALL",5.6,GREEN)]
grp=VGroup()
for k,(n,h,c) in enumerate(data):
    b=Rectangle(width=2.2,height=h,fill_color=c,fill_opacity=0.85,stroke_width=0)
    b.move_to(LEFT*4+RIGHT*4*k+DOWN*2.6+UP*h/2)
    t=Text(n,font_size=28,color=WHITE).next_to(b,UP,buff=0.15)
    grp.add(VGroup(b,t))
self.play(Write(title),run_time=0.8)
for g in grp: self.play(GrowFromEdge(g[0],DOWN),FadeIn(g[1]),run_time=1.6)
self.wait(1.2)
scenes.text: A person needs roughly two litres a day. A solar still gives a trickle, but one heavy squall can fill every container you own.

scenes.fact: Fish flesh is mostly water, but protein costs\Nwater to digest, so rain still matters.
scenes.text: Option three is fish. Their flesh is mostly water, and survival guides mention fluid from the eyes and spine as a last resort.
Alvarenga said he also caught turtles and seabirds, and drank turtle blood when rain failed.
The rule never changes. Do not drink seawater. Most guides say urine is no better, because it concentrates the same salts.
Rescue is a lottery. Ships passed both Callahan and Alvarenga without seeing them.

label: BEING SEEN
A speck on the sea
scenes.text: From the air, a person is just a speck. Bright colours, mirrors and flares are your voice.
Modern rafts carry a canopy, flares and emergency water, and a beacon can bring a helicopter.
Searchers also run drift models, using wind and current to guess where a raft has gone.
If a boat is diverted, it may be the only hope, so every flare and reflection counts.
In January 2014, Alvarenga's boat reached a tiny Marshall Islands atoll, and locals found him.

scenes.text: Quick check. How long did José Alvarenga survive adrift?

items=[("1","SHADE AND RATION",YELLOW),("2","CATCH EVERY DROP OF RAIN",BLUE),("3","NEVER DRINK THE SEA",RED),("4","STAY VISIBLE",ORANGE),("5","KEEP COUNTING DAYS",GREEN)]
rows=VGroup()
for n,t,c in items:
    rows.add(VGroup(Text(n,font_size=44,color=c),Text(t,font_size=40,color=WHITE)).arrange(RIGHT,buff=0.5))
rows.arrange(DOWN,buff=0.45,aligned_edge=LEFT).move_to(DOWN*0.4)
self.play(Write(title),run_time=0.8)
for r in rows: self.play(FadeIn(r,shift=UP*0.3),run_time=0.9)
self.wait(1.2)
scenes.text: So here is the recap. Shade and ration. Catch every drop of rain. Never drink the sea. Stay visible. And keep counting the days.

So could you survive lost at sea? Maybe. These men were not superhuman. They rationed, they caught rain, and they never stopped counting. The ocean is a desert you float on. If this story hooked you, subscribe to Oddly Logical Science for more true stories this strange.

shorts.title: 438 days lost at sea. Nobody could believe it.

scenes.text: Alvarenga survived 438 days lost at sea. Some people called it impossible.
In December 2012, Mexican fisherman José Salvador Alvarenga was blown out to sea by a storm.
He drank rain, ate fish and birds, and said he drank turtle blood. Currents did the travelling.
In January 2014 he reached the Marshall Islands, about ten thousand kilometres away.
The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

shorts.title: You are dying of thirst. Don't drink the water.

scenes.text: You are dying of thirst on a raft, surrounded by water. Drinking it kills you faster.
Seawater is about three and a half percent salt, far saltier than your blood.
By osmosis, that salt pulls water out of your cells, and they shrink.
Your kidneys cannot make urine that salty, so every sip costs more water than it gives.
The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.
One man spent 133 days alone on a raft, and then walked away smiling? Almost.
In 1942, steward Poon Lim's ship was torpedoed in the Atlantic. He climbed onto a wooden raft.
He caught rain, and fished with hooks he made himself.
Brazilian fishermen found him in April 1943. It is the longest recorded solo raft survival.
The full story is on the channel — subscribe for the next one.

youtube.title: Could You Survive Lost at Sea? The 438-Day Truth
youtube.description:
Could you survive lost at sea? Three real castaways say yes: Steven Callahan (76 days, 1982), Poon Lim (133 days, 1942-43) and José Salvador Alvarenga (about 438 days, 2012-14). We drop you in a life raft and use animation to show the rule of threes, how dehydration works, why seawater kills (osmosis), how to get fresh water, and how ocean currents carried Alvarenga roughly 10,000 km across the Pacific.

In this video:
- The rule of threes
- Why you can't drink the sea
- Three men, three answers
- How to make fresh water
- The lottery of rescue

Sources:
- Steven Callahan, Adrift: Seventy-Six Days Lost at Sea (1986)
- US Navy / National Museum of the U.S. Navy records on Poon Lim (1943)
- Press and medical reports on José Salvador Alvarenga's rescue in the Marshall Islands (January 2014)
- NOAA / NASA ocean current and Blue Marble imagery
- Standard physiology texts on osmosis, renal salt excretion and dehydration

Life raft photos: NPL FP2011 (CC BY-SA 3.0), Sillerkiil (CC BY-SA 4.0). Hydration colour chart: Petar Milosevic (CC BY-SA 4.0). Globe texture: NASA Earth Observatory Blue Marble. Video: Pixabay (Pixabay Content License). Facts: Callahan, Adrift (1986); Poon Lim records (US Navy; Imperial War Museums); Alvarenga reports (2014); osmosis and dehydration physiology.
